evidence.claim: The rocky north shore of Lake Pend Oreille sets the course
evidence.quote: The rocky northern shoreline of Lake Pend Oreille—Idaho’s largest and deepest lake—sets the route for the Pend Oreille Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: Visit Idaho highlights the lake, alpine views and forests; the Federal Highway Administration lists the route as a National Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: Pend Oreille Scenic Byway National Scenic Byway • Idaho

evidence.claim: Visit Idaho highlights the lake, alpine views and forests;
evidence.quote: Revel in impressive alpine vistas, far-reaching forests and sparkling water as far as the eye can see.

evidence.claim: Visit Idaho gives its length as 34.5 miles and its driving time as 46 minutes.
evidence.quote: Length 34.5 miles 55.5 km Time 46 minutes

evidence.claim: The Cabinet Mountains stand along the north-shore stretch, where the highway has overlooks as well as turnouts along the lake.
evidence.quote: The highway heads eastward along the north shores of lake Pend Oreille at the very feet of the Cabinet Mountains with several turnouts and scenic overlooks.

evidence.claim: This road corridor belonged to the National Parks Highway, an early twentieth-century auto trail intended to connect national parks.
evidence.quote: SH-200 was originally part of the National Parks Highway, a national auto trail created in the early 20th century to connect various national parks.

evidence.claim: It became State Highway 3 in the 1930s, then carried the U.S. 10A number from 1941 to 1967.
evidence.quote: In the 1930s, it was designated as State Highway 3, corresponding with the Montana highway's number. From 1941 to 1967, the route was signed as part of U.S. Route 10A.

evidence.claim: When U.S. 10A was decommissioned, Idaho joined a multistate effort to give the Spokane–Duluth corridor a common number. Idaho 200 followed in 1968.
evidence.quote: After that highway's decommissioning, Idaho State Highway 200 was created in 1968 to replace it as part of a multi-state effort to renumber highways on the Spokane–Duluth corridor to the same number.

evidence.claim: The Idaho 200 portion west of the U.S. 2/95 intersection had been removed by 2007, though the mileposts retained the older length.
evidence.quote: By 2007, the portion of Highway 200 west of the US 2/95 intersection had been terminated. Mileposts still display its pre-2007 length.

evidence.claim: Start at U.S. 95 in Ponderay, north of Sandpoint, and head east beneath the Cabinet Mountains.
evidence.quote: Idaho SH-200 starts at a junction with U.S. Highway 95 in Ponderay, a small community north of Sandpoint. The highway heads eastward along the north shores of lake Pend Oreille at the very feet of the Cabinet Mountains

evidence.claim: The road passes Kootenai, Hope and East Hope before reaching Clark Fork.
evidence.quote: The road passes through the towns of Ponderay, Kootenai, Hope, East Hope, and Clark Fork.

evidence.claim: Beyond town, follow the Clark Fork River valley to the Montana line, where the road keeps its number as Montana Highway 200.
evidence.quote: After the town of Clark Fork it then enters the Clark Fork River Valley following the Clark Fork River and ends at the Montana border just before Heron, MT where it becomes Montana Highway 200.

evidence.claim: In Hope, the road’s previous identity survives in its route: Highway 200 Business follows the former U.S. 10A alignment through town.
evidence.quote: State Highway 200 Business (SH-200 BUS) is a business route of Highway 200 that runs through Hope, Idaho. It follows the former route of US 10A.

evidence.claim: Hope occupies the northeast shore of Lake Pend Oreille and was home to artist Edward Kienholz.

evidence.claim: Clark Fork grew beside a railway built along the river in the early 1880s.
evidence.quote: The origins of an actual town date back to when the Northern Pacific Railway constructed a line adjacent to the Clark Fork River, near the eastern shore of Lake Pend Oreille in the early 1880s.

evidence.claim: The Northern Pacific laid its line near Lake Pend Oreille’s eastern shore; by the 1890s, a ferry service carried people across the river or upstream as far as Heron, Montana.
evidence.quote: By the 1890s a ferry boat service was used to cross the river or to travel as far as Heron, Montana, about 12 miles (20 km) upriver.

evidence.claim: The town takes its name from William Clark.
evidence.quote: The town of Clark Fork was named in honor of William Clark

evidence.claim: Its setting still joins lake and river: Clark Fork stands on the river at the lake’s eastern shore, with Lightning Creek passing just north and west of town.
evidence.quote: Clark Fork is situated on the Clark Fork River, on the eastern shores of Lake Pend Oreille.

evidence.claim: with Lightning Creek passing just north and west of town.
evidence.quote: The Lightning Creek passes just north and west of the town.

evidence.quote: After the town of Clark Fork it then enters the Clark Fork River Valley following the Clark Fork River and ends at the Montana border

evidence.claim: Near Cabinet, a concrete gravity-arch dam holds back the Clark Fork River for hydroelectric power.
evidence.quote: Cabinet Gorge Dam is a concrete gravity-arch hydroelectric dam in the northwest United States, on the Clark Fork River in northern Idaho.

evidence.claim: Near Cabinet
evidence.quote: In Idaho, just before the town of Cabinet, the Clark Fork River is dammed again at the Cabinet Gorge Dam.

evidence.claim: for hydroelectric power.
evidence.quote: The purpose of the dam is for hydroelectricity.

evidence.claim: Morrison–Knudsen began construction in 1951, diverting water through two 1,000-foot tunnels.

evidence.claim: diverting water through two 1,000-foot tunnels.

evidence.claim: Preparing the site required 32 tons of dynamite to blast rock from the canyon walls before construction could proceed.
evidence.quote: Thirty-two tons of dynamite was used to blast 50,000 cubic yards (38,000 m3) of rock from the canyon walls in order to prep the construction site.

evidence.claim: The dam was completed in 1952 in half the estimated time.

flags: Visit Idaho gives 34.5 miles and 46 minutes; archived FHWA gives 33 miles and 40 minutes. Copy attributes the Visit Idaho figures rather than reconciling unlike route measurements.
Dropped the implied certainty that the lake was named specifically after Kalispel pendants: the cache supports the translation and pendant custom but hedges who named the lake.
Omitted the current Lewis and Clark encounter claim: the town page hedges an October 1805 encounter, while the river page describes Lewis exploring in 1806; no primary account is cached.
Cached pages use Kalispel, Kootenai, Kutenai and Pend d’Oreilles in different contexts. No community-authored history is supplied, so no naming equivalence is asserted.
Cabinet moment retains its title and coordinates; the text concerns nearby Cabinet Gorge Dam, without asserting public dam access.
